title: Cecilia (22 November)
hookLine: a Roman martyr, patron of musicians

cards: A wedding in Rome. The house is loud with instruments, guests are eating and laughing, and the bride sits in the middle of it all. The old account of her life says that while the music played, she was singing too.
But not out loud. She was singing in her heart, to God alone, asking to stay true to him. Nobody at the party could hear a note of it.
That bride is Cecilia, and the silent song is why musicians, choirs and organists claim her as their patron.

teach.h: A MARTYR NAMED IN THE ROMAN CANON.
teach.b: Cecilia is one of the martyrs of Rome named in the old Roman Canon of the Mass. Her story comes from an old account of her martyrdom that reads more like a legend than a record, so it's best told as what tradition says.
She was, it says, a Christian woman of a noble family, promised in marriage to a young man named Valerian. On the wedding night she told him an angel of God watched over her.
Valerian wanted to see the angel. She sent him to a bishop named Urban, and he came back baptized. Then his brother Tiburtius came to believe too.

In time the brothers were put to death for their faith, and then Cecilia. The account says even her death was slow, and that she kept speaking of God and giving away what she had until the end. Now the music.

The Church's old prayer for her feast has a line in Latin, cantantibus organis: while the instruments were playing. The full line says that while they played, Cecilia sang in her heart to the Lord alone.

teach.h: PATRON OF ALL WHO MAKE MUSIC.
teach.b: In the old account, the instruments are the wedding music around her, the music she wasn't listening to.
Over time, people heard the line the other way round, and Cecilia became the saint of the instruments themselves: of organs and choirs, of anyone who makes music.
Both readings land in the same place. The song that mattered was the one inside. In her story, music can be a prayer, and so can silence under the music.

how: Catholics keep the memorial of Saint Cecilia on 22 November, and choirs, organists and music schools sometimes mark her feast with a concert or a sung Mass.

games.q: you're Valerian on your wedding night. your bride tells you an angel of God watches over her. what do you do?
games.why: Valerian wanted to see the angel; Cecilia sent him to the bishop Urban, and he came back baptized.

practice: Hum a tune you know, tap a rhythm on the table, or pick up an instrument; if you're somewhere you can't make a sound, do what Cecilia did and let the tune run in your head, note by note.
If you pray, make the song a prayer, a hymn or a psalm you know; if you don't, let one piece of music have all of you for a while.
